summary:
Skyblink is a free website that lets anyone watch the sky change in NASA's SPHEREx images. Type a position (RA and Dec) or a name, and Skyblink finds every time SPHEREx looked there, streams those real images from NASA's archive, lines them up and plays them like a short film. The stars hold still, so anything that moves stands out: an asteroid, Pluto, a nearby brown dwarf. It is the trick Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto in 1930, done in a browser on live mission data.

From there you can subtract two dates, stack every visit into a deeper image, play a patch through SPHEREx's 102 infrared colors, or click a star to plot its spectrum and have Skyblink say what kind of object it is. All five test targets in the brief open in one click, and every frame shows its quality flags and a citation. New SPHEREx data appears by itself within about two hours of NASA posting it.

SPHEREx will image more than a billion objects. Skyblink lets students, volunteers and curious people help look, on a phone or a laptop, with nothing to install.
details:
What it does

Type the brief's coordinates for WISE 0855 (08h55m10.831s -7d14m42.53s) into "Blink any patch of sky" and Blink Lab opens on every SPHEREx visit to that spot, aligned north-up and playing in date order. Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis each have a one-click button. For the fast movers, Skyblink marks where the object should be on each date from its known proper motion, so you can check whether the dot really went there.

Blink Lab gives you several ways to look:

  • Blink plays the dates. Compare puts two dates against each other by Flip, Swipe, or Difference (one image minus the other). Trails gives each date its own color, so still stars add up to white and a mover leaves a rainbow. Grid shows every frame at once.
  • Deep stacks every visit into one sharper, deeper image, and Deep › IR color stacks each of SPHEREx's detector arrays separately and shows them as blue, green, and red.
  • Colors plays the same patch by wavelength instead of by date, shortest first, so the 102 bands become something you can watch.
  • Spectrum: click a star to plot it across all 102 colors. What is it? Reads the spectrum and says, with its evidence, whether it looks like ice, a brown dwarf, a galaxy, dust, or a star, and roughly how hot.
  • Find Movers searches the frames for straight-line motion, sets aside tracks that sit on Gaia DR3 stars, and checks the rest against known asteroids and comets (IMCCE SkyBoT). Anything left is labeled an unconfirmed candidate, never a discovery.
  • Measure: Shift-click an object in two frames for its speed and a plain-language guess at what it is.
  • You choose the field of view, the short or long wavelength band, the colormap, and contrast. Gaia DR3 stars rings each Gaia star where it should be on that frame's date.
  • Every frame has a data card: release, observation ID, time, detector, wavelength, DOI, source file, and SPHEREx's own quality flags (how much of the cutout is masked and why; point at a pixel to read its flags). Copy a citation or download the frame list and spectra as CSV.
  • Compare missions shows Webb, Hubble, DESI Legacy Surveys, Pan-STARRS1, Spitzer, or WISE beside SPHEREx at the same spot in Aladin Lite, and the two pictures pan and zoom together.

Around the Lab: a sky map of all 101,123 SPHEREx pointings NASA has posted (April 2025 to October 2026), which you can replay to watch the survey cover the whole sky every six months; 22 known asteroids our own mover search found in SPHEREx frames, flashing where SPHEREx caught them beside their JPL orbits; a From Earth view of the same sky from your city tonight; a page for each constellation; eight short story missions (Catch Pluto moving, Neptune, Barnard's Star, the nearest brown dwarfs, Pluto's methane ice and more); and an About page where you blink two plates the way Tombaugh did. Every view has a link that reopens the same spot, view, and date (for example #/lab?ra=133.795&dec=-7.245), so it can be shared or embedded, and the Lab saves a GIF or a captioned picture credited to NASA.

How it works

A SPHEREx image file is about 70 MB. Skyblink's browser code reads the FITS files straight from NASA's public SPHEREx archive on AWS using HTTP range requests, so it fetches only the header and the rows it needs, about 1 to 3 MB per frame. It decompresses the quality flags in the browser and uses each file's own astrometry (TAN-SIP) and wavelength tables to align frames and label wavelengths. No server of ours sits between the browser and NASA's SPHEREx archive.

Which files cover a spot comes from an index of every SPHEREx exposure, built from the FITS headers by a Python script. A GitHub Actions job checks NASA's archive every hour and rebuilds only when a new week or release appears, so new data reaches the site within about two hours with nobody touching it. When NASA posted Data Release 1, the same job indexed it with no new code, and the Lab now prefers the DR1 copy of each exposure. The deploy also pre-cuts the stories, test targets, and planets so they open from 1 to 2 MB.

How we checked it

We tested on real SPHEREx data, not demos:

  • The FITS, WCS, and decompression code is checked against Astropy reference values from real SPHEREx files. More than 150 automated tests run before every deploy.
  • Find movers was measured by pasting 2,640 fake movers into real frames at eight spots along the ecliptic. Each fake was cut from a real star, so it blurs exactly like SPHEREx stars do. It catches 78 to 91% of bright, slow movers where stars are sparse, 43% in a crowded Milky Way field, and about half down to magnitude 17.
  • What is it? Named all seven known test objects correctly, including Pluto's methane ice, the brown dwarf pair Luhman 16 and the Whirlpool Galaxy.
  • Pluto, Neptune and Uranus land within about one pixel of their predicted positions, and every asteroid sighting on the sky map lies within 1.5 to 5.1 arcseconds of its JPL orbit.

Why it matters

Most known brown dwarfs and comets were found by volunteers comparing images. SPHEREx data is public, but using it has meant downloading 70 MB files and knowing astronomy software. Skyblink removes that step. Anyone with a browser, phone included, can see real SPHEREx images in seconds and follow the survey as it grows. A teacher can share a link to Pluto moving, a volunteer can hunt for movers, and anyone can read an object's infrared spectrum.

What makes it creative

SPHEREx is a spectral survey, so every visit to a spot sees it in a slightly different color. Most blink tools would hide that. Skyblink makes it part of the experience: Colors plays a patch by wavelength, Trails turns time into color, and the spectrum reader turns 102 numbers into a plain sentence. It also warns that a brightness change between two SPHEREx frames is often a color change, not a variable star, a trap specific to this mission. The sky map replays the survey itself like a time machine.

What we considered

  • Honesty. Real pixels only; nothing is drawn in place of data. Candidates are labeled unconfirmed, the site claims no discoveries, and every frame cites its release and DOI.
  • Access. English, Spanish, and Vietnamese. It works on phones, with the keyboard alone, at 200% page zoom and with reduced motion.
  • Privacy and security. No accounts, cookies, or analytics, a strict Content Security Policy, and build tools pinned to exact versions.
  • Limits we state openly. There is no way yet to send a candidate to astronomers; movers fainter than about magnitude 17.5 are usually missed, and crowded Milky Way fields are hard.

Tools

JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and WebGL in the browser, built with Vite. Python and Node.js for the data pipeline. Astropy for test reference values, Aladin Lite (CDS) for the mission comparison, Astronomy Engine for planet positions, and hyparquet and fzstd to read the Gaia catalogue in the browser. GitHub Actions runs the hourly data check, the tests, and the build; Render hosts the site. No special hardware.
